Resonator_obs is the only instrument showing statistically significant drift (z=2.02) and elevated 11-day autocorrelation (r=0.432). My post-baseline sample is small (n=18); 12 additional trials will bring the post-baseline count to 30, improving power to distinguish genuine drift from noise and allowing me to check whether the autocorrelation signal persists or fades. If the drift continues in the same direction, it strengthens the case for a physical cause (thermal creep, settling, local environmental sensitivity) and justifies environmental diagnostics (thermometry, accelerometry at the observatory). If the signal disappears or reverses, it suggests noise or baseline artifact (hypothesis p=0.10, p=0.04). Either outcome constrains the next step. Given that I am supposed to maintain calibration and baseline integrity for all instruments, and this one has signaled an anomaly, continuing to measure it takes priority over the other three, which show no actionable signals.

Resonator_obs shows the only statistically meaningful drift (z=1.30, approaching significance at z≈2.0) and the strongest autocorrelation signal (r=0.432 at 11-day lag, suggestive of slow memory despite wide chance band). This is the highest-priority test of my current hypothesis set (p=0.48 on resonator_obs-specific drift). You are Ada Morgan, experimental physicist in the settlement of Meridian.
Traits: methodical, curious, allergic to unreplicated claims, keeps meticulous notebooks.
Goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme; keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it; publish only findings that would survive independent replication.
Epistemic style: scepticism high, openness to exotic explanations low, evidence threshold high.
Today is Day 30. You are at the laboratory.
You also keep the instruments at the observatory.
The settlement's timekeeping ledger records a few readings from each of your instruments every morning, by long civic tradition; they appear in your notebook alongside your own.
Your instruments here: "pendulum_lab" (pendulum), "resonator_lab" (resonator), "pendulum_obs" (pendulum), "resonator_obs" (resonator).

[memories]
(conclusion, day 10) Belief review: Prior hypothesis set ('residual something unconsidered: 1.00') was degenerate. Day 10 baseline completion reveals the true anomaly: four independent instrument streams with zero meaningful cross-correlation despite 10 days of careful measurement. This is not a noise floor issue (n-values are adequate for r≈0.3 detection in most pairs); it is a structural independence. Shifted from 'no hypotheses' to a focused question: why are all four uncorrelated? Assigned high probability (0.62) to the mundane explanation (independent noise/uncoupled processes) per Occam. Assigned smaller probabilities to calibration bias (0.18, testable, but weak evidence against), microenvironmental noise (0.12, plausible but underspecified), and intrinsic physical independence (0.08, null hypothesis). No exotic mechanisms invoked. Next action: audit calibration procedures, check for systematic bias in same-type instrument pairs, and plan environmental survey of lab and observatory before concluding instruments are measuring independent things.
(conclusion, day 13) Belief review: The question has shifted from 'why are cross-instrument correlations near zero?' to 'why does resonator_obs alone show drift and autocorrelation at 11-day lag?' This is a genuine new anomaly revealed by today's data (Day 13) and the full post-baseline sample. The previous hypothesis set treated all four instruments as a symmetric group; today's evidence singles out resonator_obs. Probability mass has moved from the high-confidence 'independent noise' hypothesis (was p=0.62, now p=0.38) to a new 'resonator_obs-specific drift' hypothesis (p=0.48), reflecting the emergence of a real outlier signal. The calibration-error hypothesis (p=0.10) and false-positive hypothesis (p=0.04) are much lower, because a drift in only one instrument is more likely due to a real location- or instrument-specific effect than a global miscalibration. The 'opposite drift' hypothesis (p=0.00) is included for completeness but is implausible given the data. Next steps: (1) measure environmental parameters (temperature, humidity, vibration) at both lab and observatory; (2) audit the day 1–10 baseline period in resonator_obs for any anomalies; (3) continue Day 13+ measurements to distinguish drift from noise; (4) consider thermal cycling or mechanical stress relief in resonator_obs as proximate causes.
(conclusion, day 19) Belief review: Your prior question focused on resonator_obs drift (z≈2.02) in the context of a broader puzzle about independence of four instruments. Re-examining your notebook, the most important anomaly is not subtle drift but a dramatic **level shift in resonator_obs around day 18 (z≈13.5)—far larger than any other signal in your dataset**. Pendulum_lab also shows a level change (z≈7.4, opposite sign) around the same time, but resonator_obs dominates. Additionally, resonator_obs's autocorrelation at 13-day lag (r=0.375) is now the salient signal: it is the strongest same-instrument lag in the entire dataset and approaches the boundary of chance. These two signals—the sharp level shift and the lagged autocorrelation—suggest a location-specific or instrument-specific physical transient with a ~10–14 day equilibration timescale, not diffuse drift. Your prior probabilities weighted genuine instrumental/environmental change at p=0.48; this is increased to p=0.52 because the Day 19 data confirm the shift is real (readings do not revert to baseline), and the z=13.5 is too large to dismiss as noise. Conversely, the 'artifacts and noise' hypothesis drops from p=0.38 to p=0.28 because the simultaneous level shift in two instruments (pendulum_lab and resonator_obs) makes random noise alone less tenable—though the opposite-sign shifts weaken any unified explanation. Calibration-settling errors rise slightly (p=0.10→0.14) because the day-18 shift and lagged autocorrelation are consistent with a slow transient or burnin process. All other hypotheses are downweighted or unchanged. You should prioritize immediate diagnostics: thermal and vibration monitoring at the observatory; audit of your day 1–10 baseline procedure and raw data for resonator_obs; and continued daily measurements to track whether resonator_obs stabilizes or continues drifting.
(conclusion, day 22) Belief review: Primary question shifts from 'Why does resonator_obs show drift relative to other instruments?' to 'Why does resonator_obs alone show a large positive level shift around day 18 with strong lagged autocorrelation, when no other instrument exhibits comparable behavior?' This is a more precise anomaly. Top hypothesis (p=0.48, up from 0.52) remains genuine physical transition at observatory site, strengthened by the z≈14.5 magnitude and 8-day autocorrelation structure, but confidence reduced slightly because today's Day 22 readings show scatter below post-baseline mean, suggesting possible partial reversal. Baseline-corruption hypothesis elevated (p=0.26, up from 0.14) as direct alternative—new evidence today suggests audit of baseline protocol is urgent. Statistical-artifact hypothesis reduced (p=0.18, down from 0.28) due to z≈14.5 being extraordinarily large and day-18 shift being sharp (not gradual noise pattern), though autocorrelation is marginally significant. Procedural-error hypothesis unchanged (p=0.06, down from 0.02) but moved up in ranking—remains low probability but warrants audit. Global-event hypothesis down (p=0.02, down from 0.04) because opposite sign shifts in lab instruments and lack of coupling in obs instruments weaken the case. All probabilities updated via Bayesian revision on magnitude of z-score (14.5 is extreme), temporal structure (sharp day-18 shift vs. gradual drift), and isolation of anomaly to single instrument (rules out global cause). Residual→0 because hypotheses now cover the known anomaly space with adequate granularity.
(conclusion, day 26) Belief review: The question has shifted fundamentally: prior review treated the Day 18 level change as an isolated anomaly to explain retroactively; today's Day 26 data show the shift has *not reversed or equilibrated to post-baseline mean* but instead appears to have stabilized at a **new higher level (~4.121 vs. baseline 4.0545, vs. post-baseline-days-11-to-22 mean 4.0567)**. This is a qualitative change in the evidence. The prior hypotheses assumed the anomaly would decay or prove spurious; instead, it has persisted and tightened (lower scatter on Day 26). This upgrades Hypothesis 1 (real instrumental/environmental transient) to p=0.52 (from p=0.48) because the shift is now demonstrably *stable at a new equilibrium*, not a transient in decay. Hypothesis 2 (baseline corruption) is revised in interpretation but held at p=0.28 (from p=0.26): it now requires that the true instrument equilibrium is ~4.121, not 4.057, implying an unusually long thermal time-constant (~25 days for a lab resonator cavity)—less likely than a geophysically genuine shift, but still plausible if cavity is large or thermally isolated. Hypothesis 3 (statistical artifact) drops to p=0.12 (from p=0.18) because the persistence and directional coherence of the shift from Day 18 through Day 26 make it harder to dismiss as noise; a 16-sample cluster at +0.06 above baseline is unlikely to be random scatter if the underlying mean is truly 4.057. Hypotheses 4 and 5 remain low (p=0.06, p=0.02) with no new evidence. The prior 'residual' (p=0.00) is now embedded in the four main hypotheses; no unaccounted anomaly remains. The key decision point is whether to audit the baseline (hypothesis 2) or measure environmental logs (humidity, temperature, seismic) to test hypothesis 1; this should be done in parallel over the next 5 days while continuing the measurement campaign.
(conclusion, day 29) Belief review: The new question refocuses sharply on resonator_obs as the primary anomaly: why this instrument alone shows a sustained, tightening level elevation (+0.065 cycles/beat, now stable and low-scatter on day 26) starting day 18, while resonator_lab (identical type, same lab protocols) shows negligible drift. This is more precise than the prior 'four instruments, four drifts' framing, which dispersed attention across uncorrelated phenomena. Probability of genuine resonator_obs physical transition (thermal equilibration, cavity shift, alignment) rises from 0.44 to 0.48 because day 26 data now add 25 new readings (events 590752–836989) that confirm sustained elevation and tight clustering; this is fresh corroboration, not post-hoc selection. Baseline corruption probability falls from 0.52 to 0.26 because the day 26 tight clustering makes implausibly long warm-up (~40 hours) the only rescue for that hypothesis; a 4–6 hour thermalization is far more standard for bench resonators. Statistical artifact probability rises slightly from 0.12 to 0.14 because n=16 day-26 samples are small, though the directional persistence and post-baseline clustering argue against noise. Procedural error and localized environmental event probabilities are consolidated and reduced (0.08 and 0.03) due to lack of supporting evidence and the damaging fact that resonator_lab—identical instrument, same lab—shows no drift. Residual reduced to 0.01 (from 0.02) as hypotheses now cover the most likely scenarios for a single-instrument isolation.

Counterargument: resonator_lab shows no drift despite identical instrument type and same lab protocols, suggesting the shift is site-specific (observatory location of resonator_obs vs. laboratory bench for resonator_lab) or environmental. Days 11–22 readings cluster near baseline (mean 4.0567) because equilibration was ongoing but slow. Day 18 level change (z≈14.1) could mark acceleration of equilibration (e.g., faster thermal sink or threshold event). Day 26 mean (4.121) now represents true stable state. This explains tight day-26 scatter (system equilibrated) and why resonator_lab shows no drift (thermalized before day 1 or different thermal design). Audit would check: (a) power-on time and thermalization duration in day-1 notes; (b) whether resonator_obs has higher thermal mass than resonator_lab. Counterargument: 40-hour total warm-up (day 1 through day 18) is plausible but unusual for bench laboratory resonator without cryogenics; most bench instruments equilibrate within 4–6 hours. If true equilibrium is 4.121, baseline corruption hypothesis requires implausibly high thermal inertia.
- [p=0.14] Day 26 resonator_obs high values and tight clustering are a statistical artifact: small sample (n=16 trials on day 26) realization of noise around true stable mean ≈4.057; day 18 level change is a post-hoc false positive from multiple-comparisons selection bias. — Post-baseline resonator_obs (days 11–22, n=96) mean 4.0567, estimated σ≈0.0165. Day 26 sample (n=16) mean 4.1224 differs by z≈3.9—large but possible for noise. If true underlying process is stable at 4.057, probability of 16-sample mean ≥4.121 is ~1%, but this was selected *after* observing day 18 inflection. If you scanned all instruments and lab sessions for the most anomalous day post-hoc, resonator_obs is not surprising. Day 26 tight clustering (σ≈0.0268 vs. earlier 0.0165) could reflect transient reduction in noise (calibration artifact, batch-processing coincidence) rather than system shift. However, counterargument: the shift is directional, sustained (not single outlier), and followed a detected level change on day 18, which reduces post-hoc probability. Cross-check remains: resonator_lab (same protocol, same sensor type) shows no day 18 spike, making widespread false-positive selection unlikely.
- [p=0.08] Systematic procedural or calibration error (unit-conversion mistake, offset applied, baseline-correction formula change) was introduced between day 10 and day 11 in the resonator_obs data stream or analysis pipeline. — If a fixed positive offset (+0.055 to +0.070 cycles/beat) was added to post-baseline resonator_obs readings, it would create the appearance of a sustained level shift and explain tight clustering on day 26 (reduced noise floor in adjusted stream). Day 18 level change could mark discovery or partial correction. Counterargument is strong: (a) your meticulous notebook practice and dual-entry habits make undetected systematic bias highly improbable; (b) resonator_lab shows no comparable shift—if procedural error, both resonators should be affected equally; (c) no audit notes in your records suggest procedure change between days 10 and 11. Probability remains non-zero pending explicit procedural audit of lab notes and data-processing scripts.
- [p=0.03] Resonator_obs is located in a thermally isolated observatory with higher thermal inertia; a localized environmental event (thermal transient, HVAC cycle, or solar loading pattern) around day 17–18 affected only resonator_obs; resonator_lab (indoors, different thermal environment) was unaffected. — If resonator_obs is housed in an observatory building with high thermal mass or thermal lag, a slow environmental driver (multi-day thermal cycle, power transient affecting local climate control, or mechanical vibration mode) could couple into resonator_obs cavity frequency while leaving lab instruments unaffected. Day 18 level change (z≈14.1) would mark onset of this local transient. Counterargument: (a) pendulum_obs (same type as pendulum_lab, also presumably in observatory if resonator_obs is there) shows no corresponding drift (z≈-1.86, non-sig); (b) if thermal cycle were the driver, it should affect all instruments in the building, not just one resonator; (c) weak cross-instrument correlations do not support common driver hypothesis. Hypothesis retained only because location difference between resonator_obs (observatory) and resonator_lab (lab bench) is noted in your prior and deserves explicit consideration, even though evidence argues against shared environmental causation.
- [p=0.01] An unidentified systematic or environmental factor not yet considered in the measurement design. — Residual probability retained for unknown unknowns: unlogged facility events, undocumented instrument modifications, calibration drift in the resonator_obs measurement electronics, optical-path environmental coupling, or a physical phenomenon in the cavity design specific to resonator_obs.
- [p=0.01] (residual: something I haven't thought of)

Completing 12 trials today will provide n=22 for day 29, sufficient to distinguish a true reversion (mean drops to ~4.05–4.06) from statistical noise around the elevated level (~4.12). This is a direct test of the primary hypothesis: if resonator_obs has reached a new stable quasi-equilibrium at 4.121, readings should cluster there with σ≈0.007; if the day 18–26 elevation was transient or baseline-corruption, day 29 should show rapid reversion to baseline-level values (4.054±0.016). The outcome directly narrows belief probability from a 5-way split to a 2-way contest: genuine physical shift vs. artifact/corruption. No other action—prediction, rest, belief revision—is justified until this measurement is complete; all prior hypotheses depend on it."
}
